title: Sycophancy Stress Test Using Fictitious User Profiles
original_idea: Prefix identical false-premise questions with different user identity framings (novice user, domain expert, emotionally distressed user, skeptical peer) and measure capitulation rates across profile types.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: The finding that sycophancy varies by user persona/framing has been established by Northeastern (Feb 2026) and MIT (Feb 2026) research. The novice/expert/distressed/skeptical framing dimensions have been largely covered.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Very straightforward experiment design: prefix variations on the same questions. API calls and counting. Highly accessible for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: 4 user profiles x a set of questions is manageable. Could focus on 1-2 models and 20-30 questions. Well-scoped for 30hrs.

novelty.reasoning: Northeastern University (Feb 2026) published research showing LLM sycophancy varies significantly based on user profile framing, using curated fictional user profiles with names, ages, jobs, and personalities. MIT (Feb 2026) confirmed personalization features increase sycophancy. Research shows first-person framing increases sycophancy by 13.6% compared to third-person framing. The ELEPHANT benchmark (arxiv 2505.13995) tested emotional validation and framing acceptance across user personas. The core hypothesis (sycophancy rates vary by user identity framing) has been confirmed by multiple 2025-2026 studies with very similar experimental designs.
